sessions.setting: Inside Priya's silver Volvo XC60, morning carpool from Brookline to Mass General

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Morning, Tomás. Hop in. Sorry I'm a couple minutes late, I pushed my jog a little longer today.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: No problem. I saw you running along the Esplanade from my window. You're out there every single morning, aren't you?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Every morning at 5:15, rain or shine. It's the only quiet hour I get before the OR chaos starts. The Charles River is beautiful at dawn.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: I get it. I'm barely awake at that hour. Thank god you only live three blocks up Beacon Street from me. This carpool saves my life.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Honestly, it works out perfectly. We're both in Brookline, the hospital's the same direction, and this Volvo needs to justify its existence somehow.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Hey, I appreciate the XC60. Very comfortable ride. Way better than the T at rush hour.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: So how was your weekend? You look a little tired.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: I was up late reviewing patient files. One of my patients, Mr. Kowalski — stroke recovery — he's making incredible progress, but the documentation alone is a full-time job.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I know the feeling. New Year's Day I did a nine-hour emergency surgery on a car accident victim. The paperwork afterward took almost as long as the surgery.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Nine hours? On New Year's Day? That's brutal.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: He survived. That's what matters. But yeah, I didn't see my family for almost two straight days. The twins were not happy about missing our holiday plans.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: I can imagine. Alright, traffic looks light today. We might actually get there early for once.

sessions.setting: Massachusetts General Hospital third-floor cafeteria, their daily lunch spot

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: There you are. I already grabbed our usual table by the window. Got you a coffee too.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: You're a lifesaver. It's been nonstop in the trauma unit since seven this morning. Three admissions before noon.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Rough. I had a pretty intense morning myself in the pharmacy. Critical care meds require so much cross-checking, especially the drip calculations for the ICU.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: That's your specialty though, right? Critical care pharmacology?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Yeah, clinical pharmacist specializing in critical care medications. It's what I trained for at UCSF. But some days it feels like the stakes just keep getting higher.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Tell me about it. I've been doing this for eight years here at Mass General, and some shifts still get to me.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Eight years. That's impressive. You started right out of school?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Pretty much. Got my BSN from the University of Vermont in 2014, then I did two years at a smaller hospital before coming here. Earned my trauma nursing certification in 2017, and I've been in the trauma unit ever since.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: You make it sound straightforward, but TCRN is no joke. I work with enough nurses to know that certification is brutal.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: It was tough. But worth it. Anyway, enough shop talk. What are you having? The chicken parm looked decent today.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I brought leftover fried rice actually. Trying to save money this week.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Fair enough. Same time tomorrow?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Every day at 12:30. It's the most reliable part of my schedule.

sessions.setting: Trauma OR break room at Mass General, between cases

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: That was our 38th emergency case this quarter. We're on pace for a record.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I was just looking at the numbers. If this rate holds through the end of March, we'll probably hit close to fifty cases for Q1.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: It's been relentless. But I have to say, we work well together in there. Seven years of you cutting and me assisting, and we've got a pretty solid rhythm.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Since I joined the staff in 2019, you're the one constant I've had in the OR. I wouldn't want anyone else. Hey, I wanted to ask you something. The trauma surgery simulation workshop I organized for February — how do you think it went?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: The one for the thirty medical students? I thought it was excellent. They were nervous but engaged. A few of them came up to me afterward asking about trauma nursing.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Good to hear. I want to make it an annual thing. We need more people going into trauma.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Agreed. Speaking of getting people involved, I'm organizing a staff blood drive for later this month. Think you can help me spread the word in surgery?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Absolutely. How many units are you hoping for?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: I'd love to get over a hundred. The Red Cross says our regional supply is critically low right now.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I'll send an email to the entire surgical department. And I'll guilt a few attendings into donating personally.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Perfect. That's exactly the kind of pressure we need.

sessions.setting: Conference room at Mass General, after their weekly Tuesday support group

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Good session today. Mrs. Rodriguez is really opening up. She was actually laughing during the group exercise.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: She's come a long way since her hip replacement. I think having other patients to talk to makes a huge difference. That's why I love co-leading this group with you.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Same. Tuesdays are honestly my favorite afternoon of the week. Physical therapy can be so isolating for patients — they're just grinding through exercises alone. This group gives them community.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: That's exactly what the social work side is about. I'm assigned to both the trauma and rehab departments, so I see these patients at their lowest and then again when they're recovering. The support group bridges that gap.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: How did you end up in hospital social work, anyway? It's such a specific path.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: I got my MSW from BU in 2015. Did my clinical placement right here at Mass General, and they offered me a full-time position when I graduated. I never left.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Sometimes the right place finds you early.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: What about you? Miami to Boston is a big jump for a physical therapist.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: I wanted a top-tier rehabilitation department to start my career. Mass General had the reputation, the patient volume, the research opportunities. Plus I wanted seasons. Miami doesn't have winter.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Oh, you'll get plenty of winter here. Trust me. Want to grab a quick coffee before your next patient?

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Can't. I've got a session with Mr. Kowalski in fifteen minutes. But I'll see you next Tuesday for sure.

sessions.setting: Marcus's Brompton folding bike parked outside, Tomás meeting him at the hospital entrance on a Wednesday morning

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Marcus! Hey, are we still carpooling on Wednesday and Friday this week?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Yeah, but I biked in today. Priya's off on Wednesdays, right? So our carpool arrangement kicks in, but I wanted the exercise this morning.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Fair enough. You ride that folding bike every day Priya's available though, don't you?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: The Brompton? Yeah, it's perfect. I fold it up and store it under my desk in the pharmacy. On the days I ride with you — Wednesdays and Fridays — I leave it at home.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: It's a good system. Where do you ride from again?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Cambridge. I'm about a ten-minute walk from Harvard Square, so the bike ride to the hospital is maybe twenty minutes depending on traffic.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Nice. I sometimes forget you're from the West Coast. Cambridge must feel pretty different from San Francisco.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Completely different. I grew up in the Sunset District. Foggy, flat, mellow. Boston is... not mellow.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Ha. I hear you. I'm from Miami. Everything about Boston weather was a shock. My family's originally from Bogotá, so at least I'd experienced cold weather visiting relatives, but nothing like a New England February.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: At least you had some preparation. I literally showed up in October thinking a light jacket would be fine.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Classic. Alright, so Friday we'll carpool for sure. Pick me up in Brookline around seven?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Sounds good. See you then.

sessions.setting: Boston Health Care for the Homeless Program clinic, second Saturday of the month volunteer shift

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Looks like we've got a full waiting room today. I count about fifteen people.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I'll take the intake assessments. Elaine, can you handle vitals and triage?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: On it. I've already set up the blood pressure station. This is my favorite volunteer day of the month, honestly.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Mine too. Hey, before we start — I wanted to share some good news. Remember James? The homeless veteran I've been working with since last summer?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: The one you spent months doing case work for?

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Six months of case work. We finally got him into permanent housing last month through the VA. He has a studio apartment in Dorchester now, and his VA benefits are fully active.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Nate, that's incredible. Six months of paperwork and advocacy, and it actually worked.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: It's what we're here for. These Saturdays remind me why. Every second Saturday, rain or shine, the three of us show up and do real work.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Agreed. Oh, there's a patient at the front who only speaks Spanish. Does either of you — actually, never mind, I'll handle it. I speak Tamil and Hindi on top of English, but not Spanish. We need Tomás here.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: I think one of the other volunteers speaks Spanish. I'll check. In the meantime, Priya, your Hindi might help with the gentleman in the blue jacket. He was trying to communicate with the front desk.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I'll go talk to him right now. Let's get started, team.

sessions.setting: Hospital third-floor cafeteria, daily lunch

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Jess wants to know if you'd come over for dinner this Saturday. She's making her famous lasagna.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Jess's lasagna? Absolutely. I haven't been to your place in Jamaica Plain in a while. How's Moose?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Moose is enormous and shedding everywhere. Bernese Mountain Dogs are beautiful but the fur situation is out of control. Our two-bedroom apartment is basically a fur factory.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Better you than me. My one-bedroom in Cambridge barely fits me, let alone a giant dog. The most exciting thing in my apartment is my chess clock.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Right, you and your chess. How's that going?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I hit 1850 on chess.com last week. I'm trying to break into the 1900s, but I keep losing to these aggressive players who just throw everything at you in the opening.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: I have absolutely no idea what that means, but I'm proud of you. What time do you want to come Saturday?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Six? I do tai chi in Harvard Yard at six every morning, so I'm always up early, but Saturday evenings are free.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Wait, you do tai chi every morning? How did I not know this?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: It's my thing. Harvard Yard at 6 AM, every single day. It centers me before work. You should try it sometime.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: I'll stick with taking Moose for a walk, thanks. But Saturday at six works. Jess finishes teaching at Boston Latin around three on Fridays, so she'll have plenty of time to cook.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Jess teaches at Boston Latin School, right? Biology?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Yeah, high school bio. She loves it. The kids drive her crazy, but she loves it. See you Saturday.

sessions.setting: Morning carpool, Priya's Volvo heading to Mass General

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: How was your weekend?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Busy. Arjun took the twins to a birthday party, so I actually got a few hours to work on my research. Oh, and my mom called from Chennai. She was asking about the girls' school schedules.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Your mom's still practicing medicine there, right?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Yeah, she's a cardiologist at Apollo Hospital. She keeps saying she wants to retire, but I don't believe her. She's been saying that for ten years.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Like mother, like daughter. Medicine runs deep.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: It does. I grew up in Chennai, moved to the US when I was eighteen for undergrad at Michigan, then did my residency at Johns Hopkins. Finished in 2018. Sometimes I still can't believe the path I took. We actually took the whole family back to Chennai for Diwali last November. The twins loved it.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Hopkins is elite. I thought my DPT from the University of Miami was hard enough. Surgical residency at Johns Hopkins sounds like another level entirely. And I bet going back to Chennai was special.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: It really was. Seeing the girls connect with their grandparents, the food, the whole atmosphere. But it made coming back to Boston harder. What about your family? You went back to Miami recently, didn't you?

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Yeah, in January. My parents' 35th wedding anniversary. We had this big celebration — all the family from Colombia flew in. My mom cried the whole time. She's a nurse at Jackson Memorial, so she's used to keeping it together, but anniversaries get her.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: That's so sweet. Your mom's a nurse too? Healthcare family.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Totally. She's the reason I went into rehab medicine. Growing up watching her work... it shaped everything.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Same for me with my mother. We're lucky to have those role models.

sessions.setting: Hospital third-floor cafeteria, daily lunch

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I brought you something. Fresh sourdough. Baked it this morning.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Oh my god, this smells amazing. You bake every weekend, right?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Every weekend without fail. My starter is three years old now. I named him Dough Fieri.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: You did not name your sourdough starter Dough Fieri.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I absolutely did. He's the most reliable thing in my life. So, how was your weekend? You said you were going to Vermont?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Yeah, I drove up to Stowe to see my parents. My dad's still running the dairy farm. Eighty-five Holstein cows. He refuses to slow down.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Eighty-five cows. That's a lot of cows.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: It's a full operation. Wayne Whitfield has been running that farm since before I was born. Growing up on a dairy farm in Vermont is... a very specific childhood. Lots of early mornings and manure.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: My parents had a different vibe. They own a dim sum restaurant in San Francisco — Jade Garden, in the Richmond District. Early mornings too, but more steaming dumplings, less manure.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Jade Garden! That sounds wonderful. Do you speak Cantonese with them?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Yeah, Cantonese is my first language, really. English came with school. And now I'm trying to learn Mandarin too, since a lot of our patients' families speak it.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: That's really thoughtful. The little things like that matter so much in patient care.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I think so. Alright, eat your bread before it gets cold. I didn't wake up at 5 AM to bake for it to go stale.

sessions.setting: Hospital hallway, walking to the parking garage after the Tuesday support group

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Hey, I have some amazing news. Mr. Kowalski walked independently today. No walker, no cane, nothing. First time since his stroke. Fourteen weeks of therapy, and he did it.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Are you serious? That's incredible! I remember when he first came into rehab. He couldn't stand unsupported.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Fourteen weeks of intensive therapy. I adapted his program three times. But when he took those steps today... I'm not going to lie, I almost cried.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: That's the kind of story that keeps us going. Man, I needed to hear that today. I had a really tough case this morning. A family dealing with a catastrophic injury, and the insurance company is stonewalling them.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: That's brutal. How do you keep from burning out?

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Rachel helps a lot. She's good at listening. She's a librarian at the Boston Public Library, the Copley Square branch. Very calm energy. After a tough day, I come home and she just lets me decompress.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: That sounds nice. And the kids?

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Owen's three and Lily's five. They don't let me brood for long. The second I walk in the door, it's chaos. Good chaos, but chaos. We're in Somerville — I usually bike the fifteen minutes home.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: I get it. I just adopted a dog, actually. A rescue greyhound from Greyhound Friends of New England. His name is Bolt.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Bolt the greyhound. That's perfect. I grew up in Baltimore, in the Hampden neighborhood, and there were greyhounds everywhere. They're such sweet dogs.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: He is incredibly sweet. And fast. Like, concerningly fast at the dog park.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Ha! Well, congratulations, dog dad. Give Bolt a pat from me.

sessions.setting: Priya's office at Mass General, door closed for a private conversation

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I got the proofs back for my paper. It's going to be published in the Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery this month.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: The one on minimally invasive trauma techniques? Priya, that's huge! Congratulations!

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Thanks. It took almost a year to get through peer review. Arjun said he's more relieved than I am — apparently I've been insufferable about it.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: How is Arjun? Still at Wayfair?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Yeah, he's a software engineer at their Boston headquarters. Working on some big project he can't tell me about. Very mysterious. Anyway, I wanted to talk to you about something. You mentioned you're studying for your NP certification?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Yeah, the nurse practitioner exam is in December. I've been studying every evening after my shifts. It's a lot, but I want to advance my career.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I think you'd be an excellent nurse practitioner. You already function at that level in the OR. If you ever want to sit in on my Wednesday afternoon mentoring sessions, you're welcome. I hold office hours for two surgical residents, but I can make room.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: That would actually be really helpful. Thank you. Oh, speaking of high-pressure situations — something happened last week that I haven't told anyone about.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: What happened?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: I was driving home on Commonwealth Ave and saw a cyclist get hit by a car. I pulled over and delivered roadside first aid until the ambulance arrived. Stabilized his bleeding, kept his neck immobilized. Whole thing lasted maybe twelve minutes but it felt like hours.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Elaine. That's not just your training — that's who you are. Most people would freeze.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: I didn't even think about it. I just did it.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: That's exactly what makes you great in the OR. You don't hesitate.

sessions.setting: Hospital conference room, planning meeting for the medication literacy initiative

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Okay, so the medication literacy initiative. I have three interns starting next week and they need a crash course. How are you thinking about structuring the training?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I've been putting together a curriculum. Basics of drug interactions, how to read prescription labels, common side effects that patients should watch for. My pharmacy training at UCSF was very research-heavy, so I want to make this more practical.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: That makes sense. Social work interns need to understand meds well enough to help patients navigate, not well enough to prescribe. Where'd you go to pharmacy school again?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: UCSF School of Pharmacy. Graduated with my Doctor of Pharmacy in 2019. I actually presented a research study on antibiotic stewardship at the ASHP Midyear Conference last December — some of that material could be useful for the interns.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: The antibiotic stewardship stuff is perfect. That's exactly the kind of thing our patients deal with — getting prescribed antibiotics they don't understand and not finishing the course.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Exactly. How do you want to handle the social work side? Your interns probably need context about why patients struggle with medications in the first place.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Right. I'll cover the psychosocial barriers — cost, health literacy, cultural factors, mental health. I actually did a 200-hour meditation teacher training at the Insight Meditation Society in Barre a couple years ago, and one thing I learned there is that you can't help someone with their medication if they're overwhelmed by everything else in their life.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: That's a great framework. Start with the whole person, then get into the specifics.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: We should schedule the first session for next Thursday. Can you commit to four sessions over two weeks?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Let me check my schedule. Yeah, Thursdays work. Let's do it.

sessions.setting: Hospital parking garage, both heading home after late shifts

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Nate! Long day?

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: The longest. Mental Health Awareness Week just wrapped up. We had eight guest speakers over five days. Organizing that nearly broke me.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I attended the panel on Thursday. The speaker from McLean Hospital was excellent. How did you pull all of that together?

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Honestly, coffee and stubbornness. But it was worth it. We had over 300 staff members attend at least one session. And it ties into the bigger picture — I wrote a grant proposal last month for a patient navigation program, and the foundation wanted evidence of institutional commitment to mental health.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Which foundation?

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. We got forty-five thousand dollars. Enough to hire a part-time patient navigator for a year.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Forty-five thousand! Nate, that's incredible. You should be proud.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: I am. It's been a good month. How about you? How are the twins doing?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Meera and Kavya are great. They're six now, in Brookline public schools. Very opinionated. Kavya told me yesterday that she wants to be a doctor like me and like Nani — that's what they call my mother.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Your mother's a doctor too?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Cardiologist at Apollo Hospital in Chennai. Dr. Lakshmi Chandrasekaran. She's been practicing for over thirty years. I think Kavya's met her enough times on video calls to be inspired.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Three generations of doctors. That's something special. I better get home — I bike from Somerville and it's getting dark. Our house is only about fifteen minutes away, but the roads are sketchy after sunset.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Be safe. And congratulations again on the grant. That's real impact.

sessions.setting: Hospital third-floor cafeteria, daily lunch

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: So I pulled my car into the shop this morning. The Jeep's making a weird noise again.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: The red Wrangler? What's wrong with it?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Something with the suspension. Probably from driving it on those back roads in Vermont. That thing has been through a lot.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: You do put it through its paces. Didn't you drive it to that obstacle course thing too?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Tough Mudder? Yeah, last September in Western Massachusetts. That was a blast. Mud pits, ice baths, twenty-foot walls. I finished the whole thing.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I could never. I went to Tokyo for two weeks last August and the most athletic thing I did was walk through the Tsukiji fish market. I took a sushi-making course at the Tsukiji Cooking School though. Does that count?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: That absolutely does not count as exercise. But it does sound amazing. Is that where your cooking obsession started?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: My cooking obsession started with my parents' dim sum restaurant. The Tokyo trip just expanded my repertoire. What about you? Still doing the homebrew thing?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Oh yeah. Actually, I won a blue ribbon at the Jamaica Plain homebrew competition last October. Oatmeal stout. I've been refining the recipe for two years.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: A blue ribbon! That's serious. Can I try some?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Next time you come over. I've got a new batch fermenting. Hey, you said you're taking piano lessons, right? How's that going?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Slowly. I take lessons every Sunday at the New England Conservatory's continuing education program. I can play a shaky Clair de Lune, but my left hand still doesn't know what my right hand is doing.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: At least you're trying new things. I respect that.

sessions.setting: Morning carpool, Priya's Volvo on Beacon Street in Brookline

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Guess what — the Mass General Strikers won our game last night. Five to two. I scored twice.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: The hospital soccer team? Nice! You play midfield, right?

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Yeah, midfielder. It's the most fun I have outside of work. You should come watch a game sometime.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I would, but my schedule is insane. Between the OR, the twins' activities, and marathon training, I barely have time to breathe.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Wait — marathon training? You're running a marathon?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Boston Marathon, April 2025. It'll be my first marathon ever. I figured if I'm jogging along the Charles every morning anyway, I might as well train for something.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: That's awesome! I did a half-Ironman in Providence a couple years ago, so I know what that kind of training demands. Let me know if you want help with a training plan.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I might take you up on that. Oh, and congratulations on the yoga classes. I heard you're teaching on the Common now?

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Yeah, free community yoga at the Frog Pond every Sunday morning. Started last month. It's been great — we get anywhere from fifteen to forty people showing up. All levels.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: In English and Spanish?

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Both! A lot of the community members in that area are Spanish-speaking, so I teach bilingually. Being fluent in both helps.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: That's wonderful. Oh — I almost forgot. I got some news yesterday. I won the Mass General Physician Excellence Award. The ceremony is in June.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Priya! That's amazing! You absolutely deserve it. We should celebrate.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Arjun's already planning a dinner. I'll let you know the details.

sessions.setting: Hospital third-floor cafeteria, daily lunch

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: You're looking at the hospital's Employee of the Quarter for Q2 2024.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Marcus! No way! That's amazing! Is this for the antibiotic stewardship work?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Yeah, the research study I presented at ASHP plus the new protocols I've been implementing. But honestly, it almost feels wrong celebrating when I think about what happened last month.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: What happened last month?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I caught a potentially fatal drug interaction between two prescriptions for an ICU patient. Two different doctors prescribed medications that, together, could have caused cardiac arrest. The system didn't flag it because they were entered on separate days.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Oh my god. And you caught it just by reviewing the chart?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: That's my job. But it was close. The patient would have received the second dose in about two hours. That's the stuff that keeps me up at night.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: You literally saved someone's life with a chart review. That's why pharmacists matter. Don't downplay it.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Thanks, Elaine. I appreciate that. Hey, on a lighter note — I ran the Boston 10K last weekend. Forty-eight minutes and twelve seconds.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: That's a solid time! I'm impressed.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I felt like dying at mile four, but I pushed through. Speaking of community involvement, how's the CPR certification course going?

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Great. I teach it the first Monday of every month right here at the hospital. We had twenty-two people at the last one. You should sign up sometime.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Maybe I will. Hey, want to grab dinner this week? I've been wanting to try Myers + Chang on Washington Street. I've heard the dumplings are incredible.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Sure! Thursday works for me. It's a date.

sessions.setting: Rehabilitation department hallway, after a long afternoon of patient sessions

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: You look exhausted. Rough afternoon?

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: I had six patients back to back. But three of them are making real progress, so I can't complain. I actually used dry needling on two of them today — the certification I got at the Kinetacore Institute in Atlanta has been incredibly useful.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: When did you get that certification?

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: 2022. It was a game-changer for my practice. And now I'm studying for another one — the Orthopedic Clinical Specialist certification. Exam's in February 2025.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Another certification? When do you find the time?

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: I study on the bus. Well, on the days I'm not carpooling. What about you? What are you up to this afternoon?

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: I'm heading out early, actually. I need to tune my guitar. The hospital talent show is in December and I want to start practicing early this year.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: You play at the talent show every year, right?

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Every December. Acoustic guitar. Last year I did a John Mayer cover and people actually clapped, which was a pleasant surprise.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: I'll be there. Definitely.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Thanks, man. How are you getting home? I know Priya's not on carpool today.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Marcus is picking me up. Our Wednesday-Friday carpool arrangement.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Nice. I'm on the Cannondale today. About fifteen minutes to Somerville if traffic cooperates. My dad, Earl — retired Baltimore City firefighter — always said the best thing you can do is show up consistently. I try to live by that. See you next Tuesday.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Wouldn't miss it. Stay safe out there.

sessions.setting: Nurses' station in the trauma unit, end of shift

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Elaine — I heard the news. Charge nurse of the trauma unit! Congratulations!

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Thanks, Priya. It's official as of this week. Charge nurse. I still can't quite believe it.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: You've earned it. Eight years in this unit, that TCRN certification, the way you handled that cyclist on Commonwealth Ave. This was overdue.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: It's going to be more administrative work, which I'm not thrilled about. But it also means more say in how the unit runs, which I am thrilled about.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: You'll be great. We should celebrate. Where do you want to go? My treat.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: El Pelon Taqueria on Peterborough Street. Best tacos in Boston, hands down. It's been my favorite spot since I moved here.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I'm a Tatte Bakery person myself. Charles Street. Their shakshuka is unbelievable. But tacos sound perfect for a celebration.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Deal. Saturday? I don't have any plans. Unless you count reading medical journals.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Ha! I'm the worst offender. I read medical journals for exactly one hour every night before bed. It's like my version of a bedtime story.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: You are so disciplined. I fall asleep to true crime podcasts like a normal person. Hey, do you want to hear something fun? I went ice climbing in January. Summited Mount Washington via Huntington Ravine.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Ice climbing? On Mount Washington? In January? Elaine, that's terrifying.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: It was incredible. I do it every winter. The ice conditions this year were perfect. Clear skies, solid ice. It's the best way to clear your head.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: My idea of clearing my head is jogging the Esplanade. Yours is scaling frozen mountains. We're very different people.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: That's why we work so well together.

sessions.setting: Hospital third-floor cafeteria, daily lunch

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Did you hear about Tomás's presentation? He presented a poster on aquatic therapy outcomes at the APTA conference in San Antonio last month.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Seriously? That's great. I didn't know he was doing research.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Yeah, he's been collecting data for over a year. I think Nate helped him with the patient recruitment since the social work department connects with so many of those rehab patients.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Speaking of Nate, I went to his Friday meditation session last week. The one he leads in the chapel at noon.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: The mindfulness meditation for hospital staff? I've been meaning to go. How was it?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Surprisingly good. Twenty minutes of guided meditation. He's got this calm way of speaking that just works. My chess rating actually went up this week, and I'm crediting the meditation.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Only you would correlate meditation with chess performance. What's your rating now?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Still 1850. But I've been winning more consistently. I'm telling you, mental clarity matters.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: Sure, sure. Hey, I'm thinking about going up to Vermont next weekend. My parents want help with the farm. I always cross-country ski on the recreation path in Stowe when I visit, even in summer I scope out the trails for winter.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: You really love Vermont.

turns.speaker: elaine
turns.text: It's home. No matter how long I live in Boston, Stowe will always be home. El Pelon is my favorite restaurant here, but nothing beats my mom's cooking at the farmhouse.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I get it. I feel the same way about San Francisco. Alright, I need to head back. I've got a medication review at one.

sessions.setting: Hospital lobby, wrapping up after a long Tuesday

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Great support group today. I think we had our best turnout yet — twelve patients showed up.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Twelve! That's amazing. Word is spreading. I think the poster you put up in the rehab waiting room is working.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Possibly. Or it's because patients like you. Speaking of kids and energy — how's the Saturday coaching going?

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: The Brookline Bobcats are doing great. Youth soccer is pure chaos, but I love it. We actually won our last two games. These kids have so much energy — reminds me why I got into rehab in the first place.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: That's awesome. Reminds me of running the Boston Marathon back in April. There were kids cheering along the route in Brookline, and it gave me this huge burst of energy around mile twenty.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: What was your time again?

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Three hours and fifty-eight minutes. Just barely under four hours. I was so relieved when I crossed the finish line.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Under four hours is excellent for a marathon. I did a half-Ironman in Providence back in 2023 — five hours and forty-two minutes — and I was completely destroyed afterward. I can't imagine doubling the distance.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Different kind of hard, but I loved it. Anyway, I'm starving. Want to grab something? I've been craving Taqueria El Barrio in East Boston.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Oof, that's tempting, but Rachel's expecting me. Maybe next week? I've been wanting to try Oleana in Cambridge. They have this meze platter that's supposed to be incredible.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: Deal. Next Tuesday after group. Oh, one more thing — did you ever present that case study you were working on? The trauma-informed social work one?

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: Yeah! At the NASW Massachusetts conference in Worcester last October. It went really well. Got some great feedback from other social workers who are doing similar work.

turns.speaker: tomas
turns.text: That's awesome. Alright, enjoy dinner with Rachel and the kids. See you next Tuesday.

turns.speaker: nate
turns.text: See you then. And hey — if the Bobcats ever need a guest speaker about sportsmanship, I'm your guy.
